# Exploring qpAdm / qpGraph models

I think this particular mini project could have---out of every other case study
idea on offer---the most impact on you your research in ancient DNA genomics.

Both qpAdm and qpGraph techniques form a core component of nearly every single
ancient DNA paper. Yet, a lot of research work has been poured ([one
paper](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/217/4/iyaa045/6070149),
[another
paper](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/228/1/iyae110/7714968), [yet
another paper](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/230/1/iyaf047/8102970))
into delineating in which situations qpAdm works and --- much more often ---
when it either fails to work or when it's often completely misinterpreted.

If you work with qpAdm, you're aware of many assumptions and recommendations
that are made, but those are rarely backed by rigorous modeling and simulation.

**In this case study, I would encourage you to take some qpAdm / qpGraph models
you have inferred in the past (or some foundational models inferred in the
literature relevant for your work), program them in the form of a parametrized
_slendr_ model, and experiment with how robust the qpAdm conclusions are to some
of the assumptions made.**

**Hint:** You already know that _slendr_ allows exporting data in the form of
EIGENSTRAT files via the function `ts_eigenstrat()` (as introduced [in recipes
in this
chapter](haplotype-methods.html#exercise-converting-tree-sequences-to-other-genotype-formats))
which means that connecting _slendr_ simulation scripts with the
[ADMIXTOOLS2](https://uqrmaie1.github.io/admixtools/index.html) software in R
should be quite straightforward.
